newsitem.title: USA: April construction spending dips, first fall this year.
newsitem.headline: April construction spending dips, first fall this year.

text.p: Spending on all types of new construction dropped in April for the first time in four months, the Commerce Department said on Monday, though the housing sector remained exceptionally strong.
Total spending dropped 1 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $596.9 billion after a sharply revised 0.1 percent increase in March that previously was reported as a 0.2 percent decrease.

The falloff in April construction spending was the first since December, when it also fell by 1 percent. The last month in which there was a bigger decrease was nearly a year ago, in May 1996, when spending tumbled 1.1 percent.
Wall Street economists had forecast that April spending would rise 0.3 percent from March rather than decline.

Privately financed construction projects fell 0.8 percent to an annual rate of $450.2 billion after a 0.4 percent March falloff. Public or taxpayer-financed projects were down 1.8 percent to $146.7 billion following a 1.6 percent March increase.
Notwithstanding the easing in overall construction spending during April, the housing sector remained vigorous.
Spending on residential construction projects rose 0.2 percent to a record $258.2 billion annual rate after a 0.9 percent March rise.
Similarly, single-family homebuilding was up slightly to a record $160.1 billion rate from $160 billion in March.
But spending on nonresidential building fell by a sharp 2.6 percent to an annual rate of $150.9 billion after a 1.5 percent drop in March.
Spending to build new offices and hotels was down from March though industrial project spending was higher.

Government spending on construction projects fell 1.8 percent in April to an annual rate of $146.7 billion after a 1.6 percent March gain. April spending was down on schools, conservation projects and water treatment plants.
After allowing for inflation, total construction spending fell 1.3 percent in April to a seasonally adjusted $511.3 billion annual rate following a 0.3 percent decline in March, the department said.
